pr_body:
/kind cleanup

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
    
Currently kube-proxy treat ExternalIPs differently depending on
were the traffic is originated and if the ExternalIP is present
or not in the system. It also depends on the CNI implementation to
discriminate between local and non-local traffic.
    
Since the ExternalIP belongs to a Service, we can avoid the roundtrip
of sending the traffic originated internally outside, if the ExternalIP
is not present in the host and send it directly to the Service.
Also, we leverage the new LocalTrafficDetector to detect the local
traffic and not rely on the CNI implementations for this.

Fixes #95785

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

```release-note
kube-proxy: Traffic from the cluster directed to ExternalIPs is always sent directly to the Service.
```

issue_context.body:
**What would you like to be added**:

e2e test for service ExternalIPs

**Why is this needed**:

There is no test covering Service ExternalIPs

## How to test it

Since we can not assume that the e2e binary will have connectivity against the nodes
and that we can add routes to the environment, we are going to test it from a pod.

I've verified that this works locally with the following commands:

```sh
$ kubectl create deployment httpd --image httpd
deployment.apps/httpd created
$ kubectl expose deployment httpd --external-ip=19.19.19.19 --port 80
service/httpd exposed
$ kubectl run test -it --image=busybox -- sh
/ # ip a                                                                                                                                     
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue qlen 1000                                                                              
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00 brd 00:00:00:00:00:00                                                                                    
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo                                                                                                           
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever                                                                                               
    inet6 ::1/128 scope host                                                                                                                 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever                                                                                               
3: eth0@if2: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP,M-DOWN> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue                                                                 
    link/ether a2:5c:4a:79:5f:fe brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff                                                                                       
    inet 10.244.2.2/24 brd 10.244.2.255 scope global eth0                                                                                    
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 fe80::a05c:4aff:fe79:5ffe/64 scope link 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
/ # echo GET | nc 19.19.19.19 80
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Date: Thu, 22 Oct 2020 08:06:55 GMT
```

The test should leverage current framework, maybe something as
`should be able to create a functioning ClusterIP service with ExternalIPs`


A good example is here, 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ededd08ba131b727e60f663bd7217fffaaccd448/test/e2e/network/service.go#L1199-L1218

maybe adding a `testReachabilityOverExternalIP` ?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e0a51c9e6b4881df78e046d9c6daf4e6f2a11f78/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1143-L1146

@danwinship 
 why is not allowed that pods can reach ExternalIPs?

Wow, this is ancient and needs some fixing.  This is not about preventing pod traffic from reaching those IPs.  I had to really stare at it, and I am not 100% in my interpretation.

First, we recognize such traffic from "off machine" (!physdev-is-in &&  !src=LOCAL, which we should probably switch to localDetector) and steer it to the Service.

Second, we recognize ANY such traffic that is destined for a LOCAL address and shortcut that to the Service,

Implicitly, traffic destined for this IP where the IP is not local goes to the system's default routing logic. 

The reliance on the bridge plugin is awful and archaic and I will buy a beverage of your choice for whomever gets rid of that.  I  *think* localDetector can cover this, but not 100% sure

> Implicitly, traffic destined for this IP where the IP is not local goes to the system's default routing logic.

but the ExternalIP belongs to a service and we(kube-proxy) "knows" where to send it (to the service) , that is the part I'm not sure to understand, because whatever the user is doing with that ExternalIP it has to send it back to the cluster to reach the service. However, there is always context that is important and maybe I'm missing something.

Assuming we want to handle ALL the ExternalIP traffic with kube-proxy, the logic will be much simpler:
- traffic to an externalIP will be ALWAYS sent to the Service (DNAT)
- if traffic is NOT LOCAL, we also SNAT

review_comments: Switching to the local traffic detector is probably not currently a compatible replacement for this rule, since we don't currently have the physdev-based local traffic detector, right?

I think that the discussion is if this rule is correct, that it seems it is not, because CNIs not using bridges are not affected ...
what we want to do is to SNAT all the non-local traffic that is what the local detector should do, independently of the implementation

I am not sure this is quite correct.

Before this change, we try to:
1) always MASQ
2) send all from-off-node traffic to the service chain
3) send from-on-node traffic to the service chain IFF the dst is "local"
4) send any other from-on-node traffic to the network

(4) matters because the IP presumably might do some processing/telemtry/whatever and we don't want to short-circuit that
(3) matters because the result of (4) will be wrong if the IP is local

Now, most CNIs, including kubenet (I think) don't use the bridge any more so we effectively do:
1) always MASQ
2) send all traffic to the service chain

What you do after this change is:
1) MASQ from-off-node traffic if policy is not local-only (seems ok)
2) send all traffic to the service chain

Your (1) seems like an improvement.
Your (2) seems like not worse than what has ACTUALLY been happening.

This field is rather under-specified and, in thinking about it, it was probably wrong before.  So OK.  I think I am in.  I have a nit above, but I am happy to see physdev go away

I cherry picked the previous test, learning something new every day :)

https://golang.org/doc/effective_go.html#commentary

It's been a while since I've read the local detector code, but does this also account for traffic that would be caught with `--src-type LOCAL`?

Can we assume that externalIP _should_ bind locally in the same way `status.ingress[i].ip` (a.k.a loadbalancerIP) would? Loadbalancer IP has a check for `--src-type LOCAL` which accounts for host network traffic to external IPs. Should we add the same here?
Ah nvm, this would end up jumping to `svcXLBChain` anyways which would have the `--src-type LOCAL` check if traffic was local.

> does this also account for traffic that would be caught with `--src-type LOCAL`?

Curiously, NO.  It does not.  The "by CIDR" implementation will not catch hostNetwork pods.  Looking at how it is used today, it seems like we handle it specially ("// Next, redirect all src-type=LOCAL -> LB IP to the service chain") or is moot (MARK_MASQ does nothing).

I wonder if we should fix that more completely.  Awkward because there are some other rules with the same predicates (MARK_MASQ on the above case).
Shouldn't you also jump to MASQ if it is not implemented?  Pessimistic
